facts.fact: Some fish can survive longer than most without a filter, but not indefinitely; filterless setups are unsuitable for most keepers long-term.
Without a filter, ammonia builds up quickly and oxygen drops, which can cause permanent damage or death.
Ammonia and nitrite come mainly from fish waste and uneaten food and accumulate when no filter bacteria are present.
Labyrinth fish such as bettas and gouramis can breathe air and tolerate filter outages better than other fish.
Paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis) are labyrinth fish that can breathe air and are hardy across water conditions.
Japanese rice fish (Oryzias latipes) come from low-oxygen rice paddies and suit unheated setups.
Corydoras catfish gulp air at the surface when oxygen is low.
Pond snails and ramshorn snails breathe air with a primitive lung but are sensitive to ammonia.
Bettas survive short-term in unfiltered containers but do not thrive, and poor conditions often kill them before their first birthday.
Zebra danios are hardy with a low bioload but need plenty of oxygen.
Freshwater shrimp (cherry, ghost, Amano) need oxygen and are sensitive to ammonia and nitrite, so they survive only short periods in filterless setups.
Goldfish are heavy feeders with a high bioload.
Goldfish get their oxygen from water passing over their gills; most goldfish are fine at 5 mg/L dissolved oxygen or higher, and about 8 mg/L or higher is recommended for freshwater fish in general.
A guppy keeping guide says a filter or aeration is not mandatory for a small, lightly stocked tank, though it helps the fish stay healthier.
Signs of low oxygen include lethargy, staying near the surface and gasping, and unusually rapid gill movement.
Lethargy, loss of appetite and labored breathing can signal ammonia or nitrite poisoning.
Fish gasping at the surface usually point to low oxygen or ammonia poisoning.
Algae blooms become more likely without filtration.
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water, so warm indoor bowls are more likely to need extra aeration.
Small, crowded containers are at higher risk when there is no filter.
Guppies breed quickly, and overstocking can lead to oxygen shortage.
Quick fixes for low oxygen include gently agitating the surface, cooling the water, blowing bubbles through a tube and doing larger water changes.
During a power cut, watch for oxygen depletion or ammonia buildup, especially after a couple of hours, and do manual water changes as needed.
A single night without a filter is generally survivable in an emergency, but test the water the next morning.
Without a filter, a tank needs manual cleaning every day.
Without a filter, goldfish need about half their water changed daily.
Without a filter, zebra danios, paradise fish and shrimp need daily partial water changes.
For bettas, siphon out about 10-20% of the water and replace it with treated water at least once a week.
Keep betta water at 24-27°C and check pH (ideal 6.5-7.5) and temperature regularly.
Treat tap water with a water conditioner per the label, about 2.5-5 ml per 40 liters, because tap water usually contains chlorine.
A recommended betta container is 10-20 liters, with a minimum of 10 liters.
Keep guppies at about 24-28°C, change part of the water regularly and avoid sudden changes.
Feed guppies only what they can eat, because leftover food fouls the water.
Keep the container covered so the fish cannot jump out, and keep it out of direct sunlight.
Java fern, Java moss, Anubias and moss balls suit unheated tanks.
Live plants give guppies cover, especially the fry.
Aquatic plants produce oxygen only in light and compete with fish for oxygen at night.
A simple sponge filter with an air pump costs under $20 and uses about 5 watts, about $10 per year to run.
A heater for a 10-gallon tank uses about 25 watts, roughly 3 to 5 times as much as a filter, so if power is limited, cut the heater before the filter.
Goldfish, guppies, zebra danios, paradise fish, rice fish, and pond and ramshorn snails suit unheated tanks.
A new tank must cycle so beneficial bacteria can convert ammonia before fish are added.
Larger and more heavily stocked tanks are more likely to need an air pump.
Keeping a betta in a glass bowl with no filter is a mistake because toxins build up quickly.
Using distilled or purified water for bettas is a mistake.
Keeping two male bettas in one container is a mistake because they fight.
Ramshorn snails eat plants and breed quickly, so avoid them in planted setups; pond snail populations can also explode.
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so aeration matters more in hot weather. This is relevant to Vietnam's hot season, though the source is general.
During power cuts, an inverter or generator can run the filter; inverters run on batteries and are usually cheaper in the long run.
Vietnamese betta care guides advise treating tap water because it is chlorinated.
Myth: fish can live without a filter. Aquariadise calls this a myth for most setups; only advanced keepers have occasionally run densely planted filterless tanks.
Myth: goldfish are labyrinth fish that breathe air. Aquariadise says they breathe only dissolved oxygen through their gills and instead lower their metabolism in low oxygen.
Myth: bettas are fine without a filter. Aquariadise says they survive only short-term and are very sensitive to ammonia and toxins.

Fish Keeping Academy says goldfish do not need an air pump to breathe and that a pump is generally unnecessary in a small tank or bowl. The same article also says warm indoor bowls may benefit from one.
How long fish survive without a filter depends on tank size, stocking, species, maintenance, and whether live plants or air stones are present; some fish may start dying within a day.
